claim: Many channelrhodopsins are permeable to protons.
source: Many channelrhodopsins are permeable to protons.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract without specific experimental data provided in this sentence, but it represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Activation of CheRiff led to significant acidification in neurons.
source: We found that in neurons, activation of a high-current channelrhodopsin, CheRiff, led to significant acidification, with faster acidification in the dendrites than in the soma.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements described in the manuscript.

claim: Acidification occurred faster in dendrites than in the soma during CheRiff activation.
source: We found that in neurons, activation of a high-current channelrhodopsin, CheRiff, led to significant acidification, with faster acidification in the dendrites than in the soma.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The acidification was due to proton transport through the opsin, rather than through other voltage-dependent channels.
source: Experiments with patterned optogenetic stimulation in monolayers of HEK cells established that the acidification was due to proton transport through the opsin, rather than through other voltage-dependent channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by patterned stimulation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: PsCatCh2.0 showed large photocurrents but small proton permeability.
source: We identified and characterized two opsins which showed large photocurrents, but small proton permeability, PsCatCh2.0 and ChR2-3M.
evidence: This is supported by experimental characterization data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ChR2-3M showed large photocurrents but small proton permeability.
source: We identified and characterized two opsins which showed large photocurrents, but small proton permeability, PsCatCh2.0 and ChR2-3M.
evidence: This is supported by experimental characterization data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PsCatCh2.0 showed excellent response kinetics.
source: PsCatCh2.0 showed excellent response kinetics and was also spectrally compatible with simultaneous voltage imaging with QuasAr6a.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: PsCatCh2.0 is spectrally compatible with simultaneous voltage imaging with QuasAr6a.
source: PsCatCh2.0 showed excellent response kinetics and was also spectrally compatible with simultaneous voltage imaging with QuasAr6a.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing simultaneous optogenetic stimulation and voltage imaging.

claim: Stimulation-evoked acidification is a possible source of disruptions to cell health in scientific and prospective therapeutic applications of optogenetics.
source: Stimulation-evoked acidification is a possible source of disruptions to cell health in scientific and prospective therapeutic applications of optogenetics.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential implications of the findings.

claim: Channelrhodopsins with low proton permeability are a promising strategy for avoiding problems related to acidification.
source: Channelrhodopsins with low proton permeability are a promising strategy for avoiding these problems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Channelrhodopsins are light-gated ion channels that are widely used to modulate the activity of neurons and other excitable cells.
source: Channelrhodopsins are light-gated ion channels that are widely used to modulate the activity of neurons and other excitable cells (Govorunova et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Channelrhodopsins are entering clinical practice as a treatment for forms of blindness.
source: In addition to research use, these tools are entering clinical practice as a treatment for forms blindness (Busskamp et al., 2012; Sahel et al., 2021) and are under consideration for treatments of other disorders of neural excitability (Chow and Boyden, 2013; Krook-Magnuson et al., 2013; Bansal et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Channelrhodopsins are under consideration for treatments of other disorders of neural excitability.
source: In addition to research use, these tools are entering clinical practice as a treatment for forms blindness (Busskamp et al., 2012; Sahel et al., 2021) and are under consideration for treatments of other disorders of neural excitability (Chow and Boyden, 2013; Krook-Magnuson et al., 2013; Bansal et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Ionic perturbations are largest when the basal intracellular concentration of the relevant ion is low.
source: Ionic perturbations are largest when (1) the basal intracellular concentration of the relevant ion is low, (2) the surface-to-volume ratio is high, and (3) the channel is activated chronically.
evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles.

claim: Ionic perturbations are largest when the surface-to-volume ratio is high.
source: Ionic perturbations are largest when (1) the basal intracellular concentration of the relevant ion is low, (2) the surface-to-volume ratio is high, and (3) the channel is activated chronically.
evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles.

claim: Ionic perturbations are largest when the channel is activated chronically.
source: Ionic perturbations are largest when (1) the basal intracellular concentration of the relevant ion is low, (2) the surface-to-volume ratio is high, and (3) the channel is activated chronically.
evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles.

claim: Sodium, potassium, and chloride ion concentrations in cells are typically in the millimolar range.
source: Sodium, potassium, and chloride ion concentrations in cells are typically in the millimolar range, and thus the fractional changes in concentration of these ions due to channel opening are typically <1%.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular ion concentrations.

claim: Fractional changes in concentration of sodium, potassium, and chloride ions due to channel opening are typically <1%.
source: Sodium, potassium, and chloride ion concentrations in cells are typically in the millimolar range, and thus the fractional changes in concentration of these ions due to channel opening are typically <1%.
evidence: This is an inference based on the millimolar concentrations of these ions.

claim: Protons and calcium ions have low free concentrations, typically ~100 nM or lower.
source: In contrast, protons and calcium ions have low free concentrations, typically ~100 nM or lower.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular ion concentrations.

claim: Ionic fluxes due to channel opening can substantially perturb proton and calcium ion concentrations.
source: In these cases, the ionic fluxes due to channel opening can substantially perturb the concentration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low basal concentrations of these ions.

claim: The amount of charge flow required to change membrane voltage by a given amount is proportional to the capacitance.
source: The amount of charge flow required to change membrane voltage by a given amount is proportional to the capacitance, and hence the membrane surface area.
evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles.

claim: Ionic concentrations in small structures with high surface-to-volume ratios are more labile to optogenetic perturbations than are concentrations in large structures.
source: For this reason, ionic concentrations in small structures with high surface-to-volume ratios are more labile to optogenetic perturbations than are concentrations in large structures.
evidence: This is an inference based on biophysical principles.

claim: Ionic concentrations equilibrate much more slowly than does membrane potential.
source: Finally, ionic concentrations equilibrate much more slowly than does membrane potential.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular biophysics.

claim: Brief optogenetic stimuli may have negligible effects on ionic concentrations.
source: Brief optogenetic stimuli may have negligible effects on concentrations, whereas chronic stimuli with high duty cycle may have cumulative effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the slow equilibration of ionic concentrations.

claim: Chronic optogenetic stimuli with high duty cycle may have cumulative effects on ionic concentrations.
source: Brief optogenetic stimuli may have negligible effects on concentrations, whereas chronic stimuli with high duty cycle may have cumulative effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the slow equilibration of ionic concentrations.

claim: Channelrhodopsins have been shown to acidify cells.
source: Channelrhodopsins have been shown to acidify cells, while light-driven outward proton pumps, such as Archaerhodopsin 3, alkalize cells (Beppu et al., 2014; Bo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Light-driven outward proton pumps, such as Archaerhodopsin 3, alkalize cells.
source: Channelrhodopsins have been shown to acidify cells, while light-driven outward proton pumps, such as Archaerhodopsin 3, alkalize cells (Beppu et al., 2014; Bo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Optogenetically triggered alkalization has been proposed as a tool to control cell death.
source: Indeed, optogenetically triggered alkalization has been proposed as a tool to control cell death (Nakao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Intracellular acidification can suppress neuronal excitability.
source: Intracellular acidification can suppress neuronal excitability and also suppress vesicle release (Sinning et al., 2011; Xiang and Bergold, 2000; Sinning and Hübner, 2013) but has also been reported to enhance release of adenosine (Lee et al., 1996; Dulla et al., 2009) and dopamine (Cannizzaro et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Intracellular acidification can suppress vesicle release.
source: Intracellular acidification can suppress neuronal excitability and also suppress vesicle release (Sinning et al., 2011; Xiang and Bergold, 2000; Sinning and Hübner, 2013) but has also been reported to enhance release of adenosine (Lee et al., 1996; Dulla et al., 2009) and dopamine (Cannizzaro et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Intracellular acidification has been reported to enhance release of adenosine.
source: Intracellular acidification can suppress neuronal excitability and also suppress vesicle release (Sinning et al., 2011; Xiang and Bergold, 2000; Sinning and Hübner, 2013) but has also been reported to enhance release of adenosine (Lee et al., 1996; Dulla et al., 2009) and dopamine (Cannizzaro et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Intracellular acidification has been reported to enhance release of dopamine.
source: Intracellular acidification can suppress neuronal excitability and also suppress vesicle release (Sinning et al., 2011; Xiang and Bergold, 2000; Sinning and Hübner, 2013) but has also been reported to enhance release of adenosine (Lee et al., 1996; Dulla et al., 2009) and dopamine (Cannizzaro et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Changes in intracellular pH can affect cell differentiation.
source: Changes in intracellular pH can also affect cell differentiation (Oginuma et al., 2020) and metabolism (Fang et al., 2017) and survival (Beppu et al., 2014; Bo et al., 2020; Xiang and Bergold, 2000; Lam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Changes in intracellular pH can affect cell metabolism.
source: Changes in intracellular pH can also affect cell differentiation (Oginuma et al., 2020) and metabolism (Fang et al., 2017) and survival (Beppu et al., 2014; Bo et al., 2020; Xiang and Bergold, 2000; Lam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Changes in intracellular pH can affect cell survival.
source: Changes in intracellular pH can also affect cell differentiation (Oginuma et al., 2020) and metabolism (Fang et al., 2017) and survival (Beppu et al., 2014; Bo et al., 2020; Xiang and Bergold, 2000; Lam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nominally similar channelrhodopsins have been reported to evoke opposite behavioral effects in live mice.
source: Nominally similar channelrhodopsins have been reported to evoke opposite behavioral effects in live mice (Baleisyte et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The cause of opposite behavioral effects from nominally similar channelrhodopsins is not known.
source: The cause of these differences is not known, but it is possible that these differences could be due, in part, to differences in ionic selectivity.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Differences in behavioral effects from nominally similar channelrhodopsins could be due, in part, to differences in ionic selectivity.
source: The cause of these differences is not known, but it is possible that these differences could be due, in part, to differences in ionic selectivity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible causes.

claim: pHoran4 is a red-shifted fluorescent pH sensor with an excitation peak at 547 nm.
source: For the pH measurement we used pHoran4 (Shen et al., 2014), a red-shifted reporter with an excitation peak at 547 nm and a pKa of 7.5.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents a property of the sensor.

claim: pHoran4 has a pKa of 7.5.
source: For the pH measurement we used pHoran4 (Shen et al., 2014), a red-shifted reporter with an excitation peak at 547 nm and a pKa of 7.5.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents a property of the sensor.

claim: CheRiff is a non-selective cation channel with an activation peak at 460 nm.
source: For the actuator we used CheRiff-GFP, a non-selective cation channel with an activation peak at 460 nm (Hochbaum et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents a property of the channelrhodopsin.

claim: An initial pH of 7.3 was assumed for all cells.
source: We assumed an initial pH of 7.3 for all the cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an explicit statement about an assumption made in the analysis.

claim: CheRiff-expressing neurons acidified to a pH of 6.76 ± 0.35 after 150 s of stimulation.
source: After 150 s of stimulation and imaging, the pH had decreased within the neurons that expressed CheRiff-GFP, from 7.3 to 6.76 ± 0.35 (mean ± standard deviation [SD], n = 34 cells, Figure 1D, E), corresponding to an approximately threefold increase in concentration of free protons.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: CheRiff activation corresponds to an approximately threefold increase in concentration of free protons.
source: After 150 s of stimulation and imaging, the pH had decreased within the neurons that expressed CheRiff-GFP, from 7.3 to 6.76 ± 0.35 (mean ± standard deviation [SD], n = 34 cells, Figure 1D, E), corresponding to an approximately threefold increase in concentration of free protons.
evidence: This is calculated from the pH change data.

claim: pH recovery after CheRiff stimulation was slow, returning to only pH 6.95 ± 0.33 after 150 s without stimulation.
source: Recovery was slow, returning to only pH 6.95 ± 0.33 (mean ± SD) after 150 s.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data.

claim: Neurons expressing pHoran4 but not CheRiff showed a small fluorescence increase during the stimulation period (0.11 ΔF/F).
source: Control experiments in neurons that expressed pHoran4 but not CheRiff showed a small fluorescence increase during the stimulation period (0.11 ΔF/F), much smaller in magnitude and opposite in sign compared to the change in cells expressing CheRiff and pHoran4 (−0.34 ΔF/F).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data.

claim: Neurons expressing both CheRiff and pHoran4 showed a fluorescence change of −0.34 ΔF/F during stimulation.
source: Control experiments in neurons that expressed pHoran4 but not CheRiff showed a small fluorescence increase during the stimulation period (0.11 ΔF/F), much smaller in magnitude and opposite in sign compared to the change in cells expressing CheRiff and pHoran4 (−0.34 ΔF/F).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data.

claim: The slight increase in fluorescence of CheRiff-negative cells is attributed to a blue light-mediated photoactivation artifact.
source: We attribute the slight increase in fluorescence of the CheRiff-negative cells to a blue light-mediated photoactivation artifact, as has been seen in other fluorescent reporters (Farhi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with known artifacts in other reporters.

claim: Stimulation-induced pH changes and post-stimulation recovery were faster in dendrites than in the soma.
source: We observed that stimulation-induced pH changes and post-stimulation recovery were faster in the dendrites than in the soma (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The faster pH changes in dendrites compared to soma are most likely due to the higher surface-to-volume ratio of thin processes.
source: This effect is most likely due to the higher surface-to-volume ratio of thin processes.
evidence: This is an inference based on biophysical principles.

claim: For a given proton current density across the membrane, the change in local proton concentration is greater in a thin tube than in the large soma.
source: For a given proton current density across the membrane, the change in local proton concentration is greater in a thin tube than in the large soma.
evidence: This is based on biophysical principles relating to surface-to-volume ratios.

claim: Kir2.1 polarized HEK cells to a resting potential of approximately −70 mV.
source: The Kir2.1 channel polarized the HEK cells to a resting potential of approximately −70 mV (Zhang et al., 2016), providing a driving force for proton entry.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Kir2.1 has been reported not to carry a proton current itself.
source: Kir2.1 has been reported not to carry a proton current itself (Ye et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: HEK cells grown into a confluent monolayer coupled electrically via endogenous gap junctions.
source: When the cells were grown into a confluent monolayer, they coupled electrically via endogenous gap junctions (Figure 2B; McNamara et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: HEK cells expressing CheRiff, pHoran4, and Kir2.1 acidified to a pH of 6.96 ± 0.15 after 60 s of stimulation.
source: After 60 s of stimulation, cells expressing all three components were acidified to a pH of 6.96 ± 0.15 (mean ± SD, n = 75 cells).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data.

claim: HEK cells not expressing Kir2.1 had substantially less acidification (final pH 7.21 ± 0.05).
source: Cells not expressing Kir2.1 had substantially less acidification (final pH 7.21 ± 0.05, mean ± SD, n = 70 cells, p = 2e−24, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), confirming the importance of membrane voltage as a driving force for proton entry.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data.

claim: Membrane voltage is important as a driving force for proton entry.
source: Cells not expressing Kir2.1 had substantially less acidification (final pH 7.21 ± 0.05, mean ± SD, n = 70 cells, p = 2e−24, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), confirming the importance of membrane voltage as a driving force for proton entry.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data comparing cells with and without Kir2.1.

claim: HEK cells lacking both CheRiff and Kir2.1 did not show detectable acidification (final pH 7.31 ± 0.02).
source: Cells lacking both the CheRiff and the Kir2.1 did not show detectable acidification (final pH 7.31 ± 0.02, mean ± SD, n = 13 cells, Figure 2D–F), consistent with our results in neurons (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Local CheRiff activation led to depolarization of neighboring regions with an electrotonic length constant of ~300 μm.
source: Due to the gap junctions, local CheRiff activation led to depolarization of neighboring regions, with an electrotonic length constant of ~300 μm (McNamara et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Proton diffusion through gap junctions is orders of magnitude slower than propagation of membrane voltage.
source: While protons can also diffuse through gap junctions, this process is orders of magnitude slower than propagation of membrane voltage (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In directly stimulated 'Blue On' regions, robust acidification was observed after 13.5 s (pH = 7.27 ± 0.016).
source: In the directly stimulated 'Blue On' regions we observed robust acidification after 13.5 s (pH = 7.27 ± 0.016, mean ± SD, n = 26 cells), and in the indirectly depolarized 'Blue Off' regions we observed no acidification (pH = 7.31 ± 0.003, mean ± SD, n = 19 cells, p = 1.5e−8 Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Figure 2K–M).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In indirectly depolarized 'Blue Off' regions, no acidification was observed (pH = 7.31 ± 0.003).
source: In the directly stimulated 'Blue On' regions we observed robust acidification after 13.5 s (pH = 7.27 ± 0.016, mean ± SD, n = 26 cells), and in the indirectly depolarized 'Blue Off' regions we observed no acidification (pH = 7.31 ± 0.003, mean ± SD, n = 19 cells, p = 1.5e−8 Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Figure 2K–M).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: CheRiff directly acidifies polarized cells via proton transport through the opsin.
source: These results establish that CheRiff directly acidifies polarized cells via proton transport through the opsin, and that electrical depolarization alone is insufficient to drive acidification.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the patterned stimulation experiments.

claim: Electrical depolarization alone is insufficient to drive acidification in HEK cells.
source: These results establish that CheRiff directly acidifies polarized cells via proton transport through the opsin, and that electrical depolarization alone is insufficient to drive acidification.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the patterned stimulation experiments showing no acidification in indirectly depolarized regions.

claim: PsCatCh2.0 is derived from Platymonas subcordiformis PsChR via the L115C mutation and addition of trafficking signals.
source: PsCatCh2.0 (Chen et al., 2022) is derived from the highly blue-shifted Platymonas subcordiformis PsChR (Govorunova et al., 2013) via the L115C mutation and addition of a trafficking signal, ER export signal, and cleavable N-terminal Lucy-Rho signal peptide.
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the opsin's origin and modifications.

claim: PsCatCh2.0 has been used for visual function restoration in blind mice.
source: Due to its high speed and high light sensitivity, this opsin has been used for visual function restoration in blind mice (Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: ChR2-3M is derived from ChR2-XXM (i.e. ChR2-D156H).
source: The second opsin we tested is derived from the recently engineered ChR2-XXM (i.e. ChR2-D156H), which shows high photocurrent and high selectivity for Na+ and K+ over H+ (Duan et al., 2019; Scholz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the parent opsin.

claim: ChR2-XXM shows high photocurrent and high selectivity for Na+ and K+ over H+.
source: The second opsin we tested is derived from the recently engineered ChR2-XXM (i.e. ChR2-D156H), which shows high photocurrent and high selectivity for Na+ and K+ over H+ (Duan et al., 2019; Scholz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutating H134 to Q in ChR2-XXM further enhanced the Na+ and K+ selectivity.
source: Mutating H134 to Q at the intracellular gate further enhanced the Na+ and K+ selectivity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and photocurrent amplitude.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutating H134 to Q in ChR2-XXM enhanced photocurrent amplitude.
source: Mutating H134 to Q at the intracellular gate further enhanced the Na+ and K+ selectivity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and photocurrent amplitude.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutating E101 to N in ChR2-XXM boosted the Na+ and K+ selectivity.
source: Mutating E101 to N near the extracellular gate site also boosted the Na+ and K+ selectivity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) without affecting the photocurrent amplitude (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutating E101 to N in ChR2-XXM did not affect photocurrent amplitude.
source: Mutating E101 to N near the extracellular gate site also boosted the Na+ and K+ selectivity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) without affecting the photocurrent amplitude (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ChR2-3M is a triple mutant of ChR2 with trafficking, ER export, and signal peptides added.
source: To optimize expression and trafficking, we added the same trafficking, ER export, and signal peptides as in PsCatCh2.0. We designate this triple mutant of ChR2 as 'ChR2-3M'.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the construct design.

claim: CheRiff cells showed a decrease in pH to 6.98 ± 0.15 after 55 s stimulation.
source: After a 55-s stimulation and imaging protocol, CheRiff cells showed a decrease in pH as above (pH = 6.98 ± 0.15, mean ± SD, n = 170 cells), while the new opsins did not show any significant changes in pH (ChR2-3M: pH = 7.31 ± 0.10, n = 63 cells; PsCatCh2.0: pH = 7.30 ± 0.03, n = 74 cells; p = 4e−31, p = 4e−35, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ChR2-3M did not show any significant changes in pH (pH = 7.31 ± 0.10) after 55 s stimulation.
source: After a 55-s stimulation and imaging protocol, CheRiff cells showed a decrease in pH as above (pH = 6.98 ± 0.15, mean ± SD, n = 170 cells), while the new opsins did not show any significant changes in pH (ChR2-3M: pH = 7.31 ± 0.10, n = 63 cells; PsCatCh2.0: pH = 7.30 ± 0.03, n = 74 cells; p = 4e−31, p = 4e−35, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: PsCatCh2.0 did not show any significant changes in pH (pH = 7.30 ± 0.03) after 55 s stimulation.
source: After a 55-s stimulation and imaging protocol, CheRiff cells showed a decrease in pH as above (pH = 6.98 ± 0.15, mean ± SD, n = 170 cells), while the new opsins did not show any significant changes in pH (ChR2-3M: pH = 7.31 ± 0.10, n = 63 cells; PsCatCh2.0: pH = 7.30 ± 0.03, n = 74 cells; p = 4e−31, p = 4e−35, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: All three opsins (CheRiff, ChR2-3M, PsCatCh2.0) induced depolarization in HEK cell monolayers.
source: In paired experiments, we used voltage imaging with BeRST1 to confirm that all three opsins induced depolarization in the HEK cell monolayers (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: ChR2-3M passed unusually large steady-state photocurrents (1378 ± 618 pA).
source: ChR2-3M passed unusually large steady-state photocurrents (1378 ± 618 pA, mean ± SD, n = 4 cells) and was highly sensitive to blue light (effective power density for 50% activation, EPD50 = 11.6 ± 8.7 mW cm−2, Figure 3E), but had slow opening (τon = 57 ± 21 ms at saturating blue light) and very slow closing (τoff = 1950 ± 500 ms, Figure 3F).
evidence: This is directly supported by patch clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ChR2-3M was highly sensitive to blue light (EPD50 = 11.6 ± 8.7 mW cm−2).
source: ChR2-3M passed unusually large steady-state photocurrents (1378 ± 618 pA, mean ± SD, n = 4 cells) and was highly sensitive to blue light (effective power density for 50% activation, EPD50 = 11.6 ± 8.7 mW cm−2, Figure 3E), but had slow opening (τon = 57 ± 21 ms at saturating blue light) and very slow closing (τoff = 1950 ± 500 ms, Figure 3F).
evidence: This is directly supported by patch clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ChR2-3M had slow opening (τon = 57 ± 21 ms at saturating blue light).
source: ChR2-3M passed unusually large steady-state photocurrents (1378 ± 618 pA, mean ± SD, n = 4 cells) and was highly sensitive to blue light (effective power density for 50% activation, EPD50 = 11.6 ± 8.7 mW cm−2, Figure 3E), but had slow opening (τon = 57 ± 21 ms at saturating blue light) and very slow closing (τoff = 1950 ± 500 ms, Figure 3F).
evidence: This is directly supported by patch clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: ChR2-3M had very slow closing (τoff = 1950 ± 500 ms).
source: ChR2-3M passed unusually large steady-state photocurrents (1378 ± 618 pA, mean ± SD, n = 4 cells) and was highly sensitive to blue light (effective power density for 50% activation, EPD50 = 11.6 ± 8.7 mW cm−2, Figure 3E), but had slow opening (τon = 57 ± 21 ms at saturating blue light) and very slow closing (τoff = 1950 ± 500 ms, Figure 3F).
evidence: This is directly supported by patch clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: PsCatCh2.0 had somewhat smaller photocurrents (847 ± 359 pA) than ChR2-3M.
source: PsCatCh2.0 had somewhat smaller photocurrents (847 ± 359 pA, n = 6 cells), higher EPD50 (116 ± 13 mW cm–2), but very fast opening (τon = 4.2 ± 3.5 ms at saturating blue light) and closing (τoff = 17.6 ± 3.4 ms).
evidence: This is directly supported by patch clamp electrophysiology data.

claim: PsCatCh2.0 had higher EPD50 (116 ± 13 mW cm−2) than ChR2-3M.
source: PsCatCh2.0 had somewhat smaller photocurrents (847 ± 359 pA, n = 6 cells), higher EPD50 (116 ± 13 mW cm–2), but very fast opening (τon = 4.2 ± 3.5 ms at saturating blue light) and closing (τoff = 17.6 ± 3.4 ms).
evidence: This is directly supported by patch clamp electrophysiology data.

claim: PsCatCh2.0 had very fast opening (τon = 4.2 ± 3.5 ms at saturating blue light).
source: PsCatCh2.0 had somewhat smaller photocurrents (847 ± 359 pA, n = 6 cells), higher EPD50 (116 ± 13 mW cm–2), but very fast opening (τon = 4.2 ± 3.5 ms at saturating blue light) and closing (τoff = 17.6 ± 3.4 ms).
evidence: This is directly supported by patch clamp electrophysiology data.

claim: PsCatCh2.0 had very fast closing (τoff = 17.6 ± 3.4 ms).
source: PsCatCh2.0 had somewhat smaller photocurrents (847 ± 359 pA, n = 6 cells), higher EPD50 (116 ± 13 mW cm–2), but very fast opening (τon = 4.2 ± 3.5 ms at saturating blue light) and closing (τoff = 17.6 ± 3.4 ms).
evidence: This is directly supported by patch clamp electrophysiology data.

claim: ChR2-3M had a positive reversal potential of 16.6 ± 3.6 mV.
